ladder.analysis: The 2026 midterms will determine control of the U.S. Senate for the remainder of President Trump's term, with Democrats needing to flip four seats to take the majority and gain power over judicial confirmations and oversight of the administration. Analysts have flagged a relatively small number of races—spread across states as varied as Alaska, Maine, Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Montana and Nebraska—as competitive enough to decide that outcome, while a broader map of governor's races and House contests in states like Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, South Dakota, New York and Ohio will shape state-level power and the House majority. Several races feature unusual circumstances worth understanding before watching returns: Alaska's ranked-choice system and a ballot dispute over two candidates sharing the name Dan Sullivan could slow and complicate that state's count; Rhode Island's incumbent governor lost his own primary; and Texas's Senate race has become the most expensive in American history, underscoring the national financial stakes both parties are placing on traditionally safe territory.
ladder.implications: The combined results across Senate, governor and House races will indicate whether Republicans retain full control of Washington or Democrats gain enough ground to check the administration's final two years, while unusually competitive contests in traditionally safe states like Texas, Alaska and Montana may offer early signals about party strength heading into the 2028 presidential race.

stories.headline: Death toll from Russian strikes on Ukrainian aid hub and power grid rises to at least 38
body: Russian strikes across Ukraine over the past 24 hours have killed at least 38 civilians and wounded scores more, Ukrainian authorities said Tuesday. The deadliest attack occurred in the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, where at least 33 people were killed when nine 3,000kg aerial bombs struck a school building being used as an aid distribution centre. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was expected to rise, with more than 50 people possibly trapped under the rubble. The attack, which he called "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war," came as residents had gathered to receive humanitarian aid. Local officials said the aid centre collapsed from a direct hit, and that when people took refuge underground, the roof collapsed, trapping many. Among the dead were two rescuers and four police officers, according to Ukraine's state emergencies service. Three days of mourning were declared in the region.

In the central city of Dnipro, a Russian missile destroyed a hospice caring for nearly 50 terminally ill patients, the oldest of whom was 90 years old. Patients were being transferred to other facilities. A separate strike in Dnipro killed two people and wounded 18 others. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a combined missile and drone attack wounded at least 73 people, most of them elderly patients, and damaged a medical facility. Across the country, Russia struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating. Kyiv's water supply was entirely cut off due to damage to the capital's energy infrastructure, and the entire metro network was suspended. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult."

Russia's defense ministry said the attack in Komyshuvakha had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen. However, BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev reported that there was no credible evidence the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and that there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement. The UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law."

Zelensky said the attack was "yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation." He noted that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible." He added: "With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal — Russia is counting on further killings."

The Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November, the first trilateral meeting since February. US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace." Speaking in Berlin, Zelensky said it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations but that he had so far seen no indication of that. The UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level" as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles, Zelensky acknowledged, saying that while the front line was stable, "the situation in the air was not as positive."

stories.headline: White House to host Russian, Ukrainian representatives as U.S. mediates Abu Dhabi peace talks
body: The White House will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives together this week for talks on the ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, as Russia on Tuesday confirmed that U.S.-mediated peace negotiations between the two countries will take place in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said the working-level discussions in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace." Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky will serve as Moscow's chief negotiator, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. Witkoff added that American negotiators will meet this week in Brussels with European and NATO officials, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and the country's reconstruction. "We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," he said.

Separately, First Lady Melania Trump will host representatives from both countries at the White House on Thursday to discuss the Kherson ceasefire, the White House said Tuesday; she will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET. The White House described the summit as "an extraordinary moment in American history" but did not name the attendees. The session follows a six-day ceasefire that ended earlier this week in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas, allowing humanitarian supplies to enter and an undisclosed number of residents to evacuate. The truce has been credited by both sides to Melania Trump and Pope Leo; Ukraine accused Russia of using it to reinforce its military positions.

Peskov also said the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans in the coming days for a trilateral meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump, and Xi Jinping to end the war — a proposal that excludes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy has insisted that any negotiations on Ukraine's future must include Kyiv. "It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20.

The talks are the latest in several rounds of U.S.-mediated exchanges during President Trump's second term, which have often yielded prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements. But Putin has refused to abandon his demand that Ukraine accept Russia's unilateral annexation of territory seized during the nearly five-year war, which began with the full-scale invasion of Feb. 24, 2022. Zelenskyy has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's land grab would set a dangerous precedent. The diplomatic activity comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with a series of Trump administration moves in October raising questions about the United States' reliability as Ukraine's most important military partner.

Violence has continued despite the localized truce. At least 29 people were killed in a strike on a village in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, authorities said Tuesday. In the northeastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 people and forcing the evacuation of about 200 patients. Russia's defense ministry said it carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine and port infrastructure in the Odesa region. Moscow's mayor said 500 Ukrainian drones heading toward the capital were destroyed overnight.

stories.headline: US midterm elections begin as voters decide control of Congress
body: Voting began across the United States on November 3 in midterm elections that will determine control of Congress and serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s second term. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are being contested, along with governorships in 36 states. The elections come amid rising living costs and the ongoing war on Iran, which have dominated the campaign.

The Republican Party currently holds slim majorities in both chambers of Congress. In the House, Republicans have 218 seats, Democrats 214, and one independent who typically votes with Republicans, with two seats vacant. In the Senate, Republicans hold 53 seats, Democrats 45, and two independents usually vote with Democrats; Vice President JD Vance would cast a tie-breaking vote if needed. Democrats need to gain four House seats to win a majority there, and four Senate seats to take control of the upper chamber.

Several key races are being closely watched. In the House, only a few races are still considered toss-ups, including districts in Iowa, Virginia, and Montana. In Texas, Democratic candidate James Talarico is running against Republican Ken Paxton in a Senate race that polls show as level; no Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994, and Talarico has gained support from some members of the Bush family, a Texas Republican dynasty. In gubernatorial contests, Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is in a tight race against Republican Rick Jackson, and if elected she would become the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. In Minnesota, Democrat Amy Klobuchar faces Republican Lisa DeMuth, though Klobuchar is heavily favored in the Democratic-leaning state.

Midterm elections are traditionally seen as a judgment on the sitting president. President Trump’s approval ratings are at a record low, and election analyst J. Miles Coleman of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics said before the last midterms that they are ‘often a referendum on the president and party currently in power.’ Coleman told CBS at the end of October that ‘it would be a surprise if the Democrats don't at least take the House.’

The outcome will decisively influence U.S. politics for the next few years. While the president holds significant executive power, most federal decisions require congressional approval. If Democrats win one or both chambers, it will become more difficult for Trump to implement changes in domestic and foreign policy. If Republicans retain control, Trump will have a clearer path to advance his agenda.

stories.headline: Job openings surge to 7.52 million in September, signaling labor market improvement
body: Job openings in the U.S. surged to a four-month high in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday, offering a positive signal for the labor market ahead of the October payrolls report. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed openings rose by 333,000 to 7.52 million, well above the Dow Jones consensus estimate of 7.15 million. The job openings rate increased to 4.5% of the total workforce, up 0.2 percentage point from August. There are now about 414,000 more job openings than unemployed workers, translating to roughly 1.05 openings per available worker.

The number of workers quitting their jobs also spiked, rising by 321,000 to 3.36 million, the highest level since March 2025. Quits are considered a barometer of worker confidence in finding new employment after leaving a position. Hires increased by 131,000 to 5.4 million, while layoffs and discharges fell by 127,000 to 1.64 million, the lowest since March 2025. Openings rose in manufacturing (54,000), state and local government (108,000), and professional and business services (106,000).

"There are more job openings than unemployed people in the United States right now. That doesn't solve all problems, but it's a big change from a year ago," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "It's an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring."

The report comes ahead of the October nonfarm payrolls report, due Friday from the BLS. The Wall Street consensus calls for an increase of 59,000 jobs, after September eked out a gain of just 29,000, while the unemployment rate is expected to hold at 4.2%. In other economic news Tuesday, September factory orders for manufactured goods jumped 1.8%, well above the 1.3% estimate and up from a 0.3% increase in August.

stories.headline: Apple stock drops on weak margin forecast in Ternus' first earnings report
body: Apple shares slid 3% in extended trading Monday after the company beat fiscal fourth-quarter revenue and earnings estimates but issued a disappointing gross margin forecast for the current quarter. Apple reported earnings per share of $2.10 versus the $1.99 expected by analysts, and revenue of $114.48 billion against the $113.39 billion forecast, according to LSEG. The quarter's revenue rose 12% from $102.5 billion a year earlier, and Apple said the period capped off its "best fiscal year ever."

The quarter's results were mixed across product lines. iPhone revenue came in at $57.58 billion versus the $56.54 billion estimate, and Mac revenue reached $10.79 billion, beating the $9.61 billion forecast. However, iPad revenue of $6.23 billion fell short of the $6.7 billion expectation, and Wearables, Home and Accessories revenue of $8.3 billion missed the $9.06 billion estimate. Other Products revenue was $31.57 billion, essentially in line with the $31.58 billion forecast, and gross margin of 47.9% topped the 47.5% estimate.

The report was the first since John Ternus took over as CEO on Sept. 1, succeeding Tim Cook. Apple said on its earnings call that it expects December-quarter revenue to rise between 7% and 10% annually, ahead of the 6.1% average analyst estimate. But its gross margin forecast for the current quarter of 45% to 46% trails the 46.3% average estimate, a key factor in the stock's decline.

Apple is contending with a global memory crunch and rising component costs. The company said memory costs were higher in the September quarter than in the June period, and it "reluctantly" raised prices across its product lineup in June, including a $100 increase on iPhones, to offset component costs. Tariff refunds added 5 cents to earnings per share. Ternus told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that growth came despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds, adding, "I think at this point, with everything we've achieved, it just feels like we've never been more confident that the best is yet to come."
The quarter included only eight days of sales of the new iPhone 18 Pro, and Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, did not reach store shelves until after the period ended.

stories.headline: NFL trade deadline: Bears land Jeffery Simmons, Colts rebuild, rumors swirl
body: The 2026 NFL trade deadline has reshaped the league with a series of blockbuster moves, headlined by the Chicago Bears' acquisition of All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans. The Bears sent the Titans a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 first-round pick, and a 2027 fourth-round pick in exchange for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Simmons made an immediate impact in his Chicago debut, recording a sack and a team-high six tackles in a 34-17 road win over the Seahawks. The trade signals the Bears' belief that their roster is ready to compete for a Super Bowl, while the Titans, now holding two future first-round picks, face questions about whether to use them on a new quarterback as they deepen their rebuild.

The Indianapolis Colts emerged as the most aggressive sellers, trading two star players on Oct. 27. The Seattle Seahawks acquired six-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, marking the fourth consecutive year Seattle has made a major midseason addition. The Seahawks hope Nelson will elevate a struggling run game, though his debut ended in a loss to the Bears. Later that day, the San Francisco 49ers reunited with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, sending the Colts a 2027 fourth-round pick. Buckner, who began his career with the 49ers as a 2016 first-round pick, returns to bolster a defensive line hit by injuries to CJ West (bone chip in knee, injured reserve) and Alfred Collins (torn patellar tendon, out for the year). The Colts received a Day 3 pick for the 32-year-old Buckner, who was on an expiring contract and had grown frustrated with Indianapolis' struggles.

Other notable trades include the Houston Texans acquiring wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. and a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Arizona Cardinals for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick. Harrison, reunited with his college quarterback C.J. Stroud, has been mostly underwhelming in his first two games but caught a touchdown in Week 7. The Cardinals admitted the former first-round pick was a poor fit in their system but secured a second-rounder in return. The Baltimore Ravens addressed their interior offensive line by acquiring Cam Jurgens and a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Philadelphia Eagles for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick. The move allows the Ravens to move Olaivavega Ioane from center to right guard and provides a long-term replacement for Tyler Linderbaum. The Eagles, mired in a six-game losing streak, are now facing a rebuild after also seeing tackle Lane Johnson and position coach Jeff Stoutland retire.

The Dallas Cowboys acquired cornerback Joey Porter Jr. from the Pittsburgh Steelers for a 2028 second-round pick and a conditional 2027 sixth-round pick that vested after Porter played two games. Porter has allowed a 39.6 passer rating on 11 targets in his first four games, but the Cowboys' defense remains in shambles, and Porter is set to become a free agent this offseason. The Steelers, unwilling to meet Porter's contract demands, secured a second-rounder as the next-best return. The New York Giants, desperate for quarterback help after Jaxson Dart tore knee ligaments in Week 2, acquired J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 fifth-round pick. McCarthy, who had fallen to third on Minnesota's depth chart, has since earned the starting job over Jameis Winston and delivered a road win over the Texans, placing the Giants in command of the NFC East.

With one week remaining until the Nov. 10 deadline, trade watch continues for a myriad of stars on struggling teams, including Jonathan Taylor, Khalil Mack, and George Pickens. The Arizona Cardinals, at 3-5, are at the forefront of rumors, with star pass rusher Josh Sweat potentially on the move. According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, Sweat would be open to a trade, and multiple teams have interest, but the Cardinals' asking price is believed to be high—reportedly a second-round pick or equivalent. Arizona has given the impression it is fine keeping Sweat if the price is not met. As contenders and pretenders become clearer, a flurry of moves is expected in the coming days as teams gear up for the home stretch or look ahead to the future.

stories.headline: Child dies of measles in New York, seventh U.S. death this year as outbreaks spread
body: A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday. The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles north of Syracuse, Gov. Kathy Hochul said. The death is the seventh measles-associated death reported in the U.S. this year; the other six were in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing a dramatic outbreak of more than 1,430 cases. Prior to this year, Pennsylvania had not seen a measles-related death in 35 years.

The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Indiana has now recorded more than 100 confirmed measles cases for the first time in the 21st century, jumping from eight cases on Sept. 2 to 104. Nearly a quarter of those infected have been hospitalized, according to epidemiologist Thomas Duszynski of IU Indianapolis. “Measles hasn’t changed. What has changed is we’ve left gaps in our vaccination status,” Duszynski said. Riley Hospital for Children is now screening patients and visitors for symptoms and exposure.

The resurgence of vaccine-preventable diseases is fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. One of the most prominent anti-vaccine activists in the U.S., Robert F. Kennedy Jr., now serves as health secretary. Since taking office, Kennedy has waged a multi-front war on vaccines, including dismantling federal vaccine recommendations and continuing to spread misinformation. Days before the New York death, The Washington Post reported that career scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention—under Kennedy’s control—were blocked from publishing an urgent health alert to clinicians about the risk and management of measles cases during pregnancy.

In a statement, Gov. Hochul directly tied the child’s death to federal policies, calling it “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” She declared a disaster emergency in early October that expanded the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics and midwives, and allowed nurses to order testing. Overall, New York has reported 170 measles cases in over a dozen counties. Experts stress that vaccination is the only way to control the disease. “The risks of getting the disease and a bad outcome are much higher than getting vaccinated,” Duszynski said.

stories.headline: FDA grants tentative approval to first generic HIV prevention shot
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted tentative approval to Dr. Reddy's Laboratories for the first generic version of lenacapavir, a groundbreaking twice-yearly injectable HIV prevention drug, just 16 months after the originator product was approved. The decision is a key step in widening access to the medicine across 120 low- and middle-income countries, where it will be available at $40 per person per year, a price comparable to daily preventive tablets. Initial supplies are expected to reach countries before the end of 2026, with broader availability in 2027.

Lenacapavir, sold as Yetzugo by Gilead Sciences in the U.S., was approved by the FDA in June 2025 and is widely seen as a game-changing tool for HIV prevention because one injection every six months provides virtually complete protection against contracting the virus. The generic was developed by Dr. Reddy's with financial, technical, and regulatory support from Unitaid, Wits RHI, and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI), following a landmark pricing agreement announced in September 2025. Gilead granted voluntary licenses for lenacapavir to six generic manufacturers, including Dr. Reddy's, in late 2024.

The rapid approval came through a novel regulatory strategy: Dr. Reddy's combined lenacapavir's two indications, HIV prevention and HIV treatment, in a single application filed through the FDA's 505(b)(2) pathway, which allowed the agency to grant a priority review targeting a decision within six months. The tentative approval is the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent and enables procurement by the U.S. government. Alongside Gilead's early voluntary licensing and the partners' support, the approach compressed a process that would typically take many years.

Demand for the drug is already strong. More than 125,000 people in 10 early-adopter African countries have started on Gilead's lenacapavir even before generic availability. “For someone at risk of HIV, taking a pill every day to prevent a disease they don't have is a hard thing to ask. Two injections a year, of a product that is almost 100% effective at preventing HIV, changes that entirely,” said CHAI CEO Dr. Neil Buddy Shah. “Getting a generic approved just 16 months after the originator, rather than a decade later, shows what's possible when we prioritize access from the start. This should be the new standard for global health.”

Unitaid Executive Director Dr. Philippe Duneton said early risk-taking is helping shorten the time between scientific breakthrough and real access, adding: “Now, with lenacapavir, we have helped shorten that timeline to just over a year. For young women in Africa, this translates into faster access to a groundbreaking HIV prevention option, with the potential to avert countless infections and drive meaningful change in the HIV response.” Deepak Sapra, Chief Executive Officer of API and Services at Dr. Reddy's, called the approval “a moment of immense pride,” while Professor Saiqa Mullick, Director of Implementation Science at Wits RHI, cautioned that “an affordable drug alone is not enough,” stressing that countries need ready health systems, confident providers, and engaged communities to ensure equitable access and impact.

The approval is “a milestone, not the finish line,” according to Unitaid. Unitaid, Wits RHI, and CHAI are working with governments, communities, the Global Fund, the U.S. Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy, and the Gates Foundation to turn approval into access on the ground, including supporting country introduction, community engagement, and generation of real-world evidence to inform how lenacapavir can best reach diverse and underserved populations. The tentative approval also provides a regulatory foundation that can accelerate national regulatory approvals and allow countries to move faster toward introduction.

stories.headline: Compass Pathways says psilocybin depression drug filing imminent after stock drop on rival's submission
body: Compass Pathways expects to complete a rolling submission of its psilocybin depression drug COMP360 to the Food and Drug Administration “in the next two weeks,” the company said Tuesday, after its stock fell more than 35% on Monday following news that the nonprofit Usona Institute had submitted its own psilocybin candidate for FDA approval. Compass shares rebounded somewhat after the announcement but remained 23% below the start of the week at $9.01 as of publication.

Both Compass and Usona hold Commissioner’s National Priority Vouchers (CNPVs) for their candidates—COMP360 for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and Usona’s PSIL201 for major depressive disorder (MDD)—which reduce FDA review periods from 10–12 months to 1–2 months. Stifel analysts said in a note Tuesday that the CNPV “gives us more confidence approval [for COMP360] should firmly come within the 1Q27 timeframe (if not earlier) based on prior CNPV timelines.” Compass said it is “on track” for a launch in the first half of 2027, subject to FDA approval.

In the Phase 3 COMP006 trial, Compass reported in August that 39% of patients with TRD who received two fixed doses of COMP360 achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in depression severity by week six, with a durable response maintained through week 26. Treatment-emergent adverse events were transient and typically occurred on the day of dosing. Usona’s PSIL201, by contrast, targets MDD rather than TRD, and its Phase 3 data have never been disclosed. In a Phase 2 placebo-controlled trial of 104 adults with MDD published in JAMA in 2023, a 25-mg dose of PSIL201 met the primary endpoint with a “rapid and sustained antidepressant effect” compared with active placebo and no serious treatment-emergent adverse events.

Stifel analysts said the Usona filing “will be an overhang for a bit, though CMPS remains confident with NDA completion imminent.” They noted that Compass emphasized that its COMP360 data are “inherently differentiated in that they come from a highly refractory TRD population.” RBC Capital Markets analysts suggested the stock dip created a buying opportunity, writing Monday that “given the size of the market - we think there is room for multiple competitors” and that “even modest commercial success is not being priced in to shares at these levels.”

stories.headline: Washington state resident dies from bird flu after exposure to infected cattle
body: A person in Washington state has died from complications of bird flu after exposure to infected cattle, marking the first such U.S. death in a year and the third overall since the virus became a major public health concern in 2024. The Yakima County resident, who had underlying health conditions, was hospitalized and died Sunday, according to county health officials. The infection was caused by the H5N1 strain of the virus, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said.

The person was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle. Yakima County officials reported that 33 dairy herds have recently tested positive for H5N1, and three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy. The Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to identify and monitor close contacts for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows, and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. However, there is no known person-to-person spread, and the risk to the general public remains low.

The two previous U.S. deaths tied to bird flu occurred in January 2025 (an elderly person in Louisiana with H5N1) and in November 2025 (a Washington state resident with a rarer version, H5N5). The recent death is the first in a year.

The CDC analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the Washington patient and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a spokesperson said Monday. Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered at higher risk.

stories.headline: UK warns AI-powered cyberattacks on critical infrastructure likely by 2028
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on AP
body: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned that AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be used in a ransomware attack against the country's critical national infrastructure (CNI) by 2028. The warning, published in the NCSC's annual review, covers facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance. The NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack on CNI between now and 2028, and also warned that Russia and China will begin using AI "routinely" in cyber-attacks.

Ransomware, a signature tactic of criminal gangs often operating out of former Soviet Union states, involves encrypting a victim's files with malicious software and demanding a cryptocurrency payment to unlock the systems and return stolen data. UK ransomware victims have included Royal Mail, outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils. The NCSC said AI will enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers scout targets, locate weaknesses in IT networks and write malicious code.

NCSC chief executive Richard Horne is set to warn in a speech accompanying the review that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently. "In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents," he will say. Horne will attribute the threat to AI's ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been "tolerated for far too long". He will also note that communications networks used by the British military face daily "persistent" and "sustained" attacks, with Russia among the perpetrators, though Moscow has deliberately kept these attacks below the threshold of armed conflict as part of its hybrid warfare strategy.

Horne will cite recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe, where hackers raised temperatures to over 50C, as a warning for companies to invest strongly in cyber resilience. "For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap," he will say. The warning follows the UK government's launch last month of the "Be Ready" campaign, which urged households to stockpile nine litres of bottled water and three days' worth of food to survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said at the time that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of "state-sponsored terrorism" by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.

Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said the NCSC's warning underscores the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology. "AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don't get the access the bad guys will beat them to it," he said. Leading AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have already given some organisations advanced access to their most powerful models to help identify serious IT glitches. An example of AI's capacity to root out previously undetected vulnerabilities came last month, when the technology helped discover a critical weakness in PHP, a computer language used by nearly 70% of the world's websites.

stories.headline: Anthropic's compute costs ate 58% of revenue in Q3 as IPO filing shows margins worsening
body: Anthropic's latest financial disclosure shows the AI company's compute costs consuming an even larger share of its revenue as it inches toward a possible IPO. In a Monday filing updating its S-1, the company reported revenue of $17 billion for the quarter ending September 30, up from $11.5 billion in the prior quarter, suggesting durable growth. But compute consumed 58% of revenue in the new quarter, up from 48% the quarter before, and the operating loss widened at the same time.

The filing extends financial disclosures that had previously covered only through June 30, giving investors a fuller view of the economics of compute at one of the major AI labs. Compute spending reached $10 billion in the quarter, including, as the filing notes, '$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.' A chart in the filing shows revenue generated for each dollar spent on compute peaked at just over 2x during the past quarter before falling back to 1.72x.

To keep up with demand growing faster than its long-term capacity, Anthropic has had to scramble for compute at higher rates. The company has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multi-billion dollar deals with Nscale, Akamai and Volta. In the parlance of the industry, those are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher prices.

Anthropic said the higher-cost picture is unlikely to change soon. 'We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute,' the filing says. The company has been working to build its own compute base under a project called Anthropic Direct, but those efforts will not be able to keep pace with demand, leaving neoclouds as the best available option.

The worsening margins amount to champagne problems: with revenue growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few IPO investors are likely to balk immediately, and a slowdown in demand would brighten the cost picture. Still, the disclosure underscores how dependent Anthropic and other AI labs remain on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout, and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in it. If bond markets get skittish or local opposition to data centers intensifies, Anthropic would have little it could do — and an already messy compute picture would get messier. In the meantime, its future will be at the mercy of compute prices.
